items.question: What do you find remarkable about the relational foundation model you recently released?
items.object: The second version of the relational foundation model
items.answer: The recent breakthrough that we had and we just released, the second version, is what we call a relational foundation model. It's a pre-trained foundation model that can reason over structured relational data. It's crazy what this model can do. It can make accurate predictions on any database and any predictive task without any model training.
quotes: To the recent breakthrough that we had and we just released, the second version is what we call a relational foundation model. It's a pre-trained foundation model that can reason over structured relational data. It's crazy what this model can do. It can make accurate predictions on any database and any predictive task without any model training.

rubrics.text: The response states that the pretrained relational foundation model can make accurate predictions on any database and predictive task without additional model training.

items.question: How do you think about building representations of patients through your AI Virtual Cell project?
items.object: AI Virtual Cell and hierarchical biomedical foundation models
items.answer: In AI Virtual Cell, we are basically building next-generation foundation models that allow us to represent human cells, patients, as well as individual molecules in cells, and allow us to reason across this complex biomedical data for discovering new cancer therapies, molecule design, reasoning about all different biomedical data modalities, objects, and how they interact with each other to help speed up science. So, it's everything from foundation models at the lower level of understanding proteins to models that aggregate the molecules in the cell to represent a single cell. And then the next-level models that say, "Oh, a tissue or a patient is a collection of cells. Cells are a collection of molecules." Let's build models that just aggregate all this knowledge in a very faithful representation, let's say, of a patient. That helps a lot because now the representations we have are much more robust, driven purely from the data. No biology, in some senses, is inserted in the model. Everything is emergent out of the data. It's amazing how much we can learn from that.

items.question: What do you find scientifically exciting about building patient representations by aggregating information from proteins into cells and from cells into patients?
items.object: Self-supervised representations of patients built from proteins and cells
items.answer: So, the way we are doing it right now is actually, the first scientific question was: is this even possible? Could you say a cell is a representation of molecules that are inside the cell? Let's say molecules inside the cell are the proteins. I can use the protein language model to represent every protein in the cell, and now the cell needs to aggregate information from all these proteins to say, "I am a cell, this is my state." Now that you have a representation of the cell, you can build a patient-level model that says a patient is a collection of cells in given states that are composed from the proteins that are in there. Can we collect this information over these orders of magnitude different scales to get a strong data-driven representation of the underlying patient in this example? The interesting thing is that this is purely doable and it's trained purely in an unsupervised, self-supervised way. You don't need to insert any human bias, any human knowledge of biology. The biology emerges from the data itself. Cell types, cell states, relationships between them, that kind of human biology, how we describe it, actually emerges directly from the data. The model learns how to best describe the underlying processes and phenomena without us pushing it on it from the top. That's the exciting, interesting, emergent capability.

items.question: What makes single-cell RNA-seq data interesting to you as a basis for representing cells?
items.object: Single-cell RNA-seq data combined with protein information
items.answer: The data we are using in this case is called single cell RNA-seq data. This is data that large international consortia are collecting. What it says is that you can take some sample from some tissue and then for every cell in that sample, you measure the number of different protein molecules inside that cell. So every cell is represented by a 20,000-dimensional vector that tells me the abundance of that specific protein in that specific cell. Every cell has different ratios of these proteins depending on its type, depending on its state, and things like that. So that's the raw input data. And then, of course, because we know what the protein is, we can actually bring the protein information through ESM or through AlphaFold. And then it gets very interesting.

items.question: Why do you see a digital twin of a single drop of blood as useful for understanding a patient's health?
items.object: A digital twin of a single drop of blood
items.answer: We can connect this all the way to the phenotype because what we are doing now is we can take a single drop of blood from a patient and then, rather than running a classical blood screen, we can do this single cell RNA-seq analysis. So now we can profile every single cell inside the drop of blood. Blood is interesting because it circulates through the entire body; it kind of captures the immune state of the entire body. So we are able to detect diseases, understand patient trajectories, and things like that just from this digital twin of a single drop of blood.

items.question: How do you see the connection between your work on human behavior, biology, and enterprise relational data?
items.object: Networks as a common framework for studying human behavior, biology, and enterprise relational data
items.answer: So, what I'm excited about, fundamentally, or how I approach things, is to always take them apart and understand how different parts interact and how different parts work together. Where I started doing this was in a science domain, computational social science. I was very excited about how people interact with each other. When I started my research career, social media just started as a phenomenon. My view at that point was: I can use social media as a telescope into human behaviors. I can study human behavior through these digital traces that people produce through using cell phones, social media, and so on. It's all about networks, graphs of people interacting with each other. What that allowed us to do, for example, is not only understand phenomena on social media, but also model the spread of COVID pandemic super accurately. We were able to computationally analyze and predict how the virus will spread as we reopen the economy. If we increase the occupancy levels at different restaurants, gyms, churches, whatever the locations, we can say, "This is how the virus would spread. This is what you can do." And underlying that was a network. So now, what is biology? Biology is a network. It's all about molecules coming together to do something in a cell. And what is a tissue? It's again cells coming together, talking to each other, organizing in a given way so that my skin has a given structure, it has a given set of layers, and so on. So that's essentially a network, a graph of interactions as well. And then you mentioned relational data: data that sits in tables in a database that every enterprise in the world has, and it's the most valuable data. That's also a graph capturing interactions of different entities inside that organization.

items.question: Why do you think AI has yet to transform structured tabular data as fundamentally as computer vision and natural language understanding?
items.object: AI's impact on structured tabular data
items.answer: What I would argue is that AI has not transformed the structured data space in the same way as computer vision or natural language understanding have been fundamentally transformed by AI. If we think about machine learning, it hasn't really changed over the last 30 years. We used to have decision trees, then support vector machines, then logistic regression, then deep neural networks, then gradient-boosted trees, and things like that. But fundamentally, it's always been: you have your data, you feature engineer this single table of your features, you add a label, and now you train some supervised model that predicts that label from the features. We've been doing that over and over again. Maybe this predictive model is a deep model, a neural network. What was the big breakthrough both in computer vision and in natural language understanding? It was: let's build neural networks that learn directly on the raw data. In the old days, in computer vision, you would do all kinds of feature engineering, SIFT features, Gabor filters, and describe the image as well as you can so you can predict whether there's a car in the image or not. In NLP, it was similar. IBM won Jeopardy with their system, but it was all super hand-engineered, manual, and so on. It worked, but it took 300 people to build it, and it was very brittle. Transformers just learn over tokens. No grammar, no syntax, it's just learning over tokens: a neural network directly on the raw data. The same thing is not happening on structured tabular data. There, we don't learn on raw data. We run all these SQL queries, all these ETL, all this feature engineering to come up with a set of signals from which we try to predict something.

items.question: How do you think about representing a relational database so a neural network can learn directly from its multiple tables?
items.object: Representing relational databases as graphs for relational deep learning
items.answer: When we came up with this idea of relational deep learning, our goal was to fundamentally disrupt this and say, "Hey, why can't I just learn directly over all relational data? Why do we always have to learn over a single data in a single table?" The point is that as I take this multi-tabular data—and to be very precise, what's a good example of this? It could be a set of customers, a set of products, so these are two tables. Each customer has an ID, each product has an ID, and maybe I have a search table that's a set of transactions that says customer ID this, bought product ID that, at this time for this price, for example. That's a three-table, super simple schema, and organizations have schemas of 50, 60 tables and more, depending on their complexity. Our question was: how could I just learn directly with a neural network over this multi-tabular data? The answer is surprisingly simple: think of the database, think of these tables as a graph of relationships between the entities in the database. I'm a graph person, so I like to think in terms of graphs. Graphs are composed of vertices, the nodes. This would be my users, my products, my transactions, and so on. These are the nodes, and the connections say this user ID was part of this transaction that was part of that product. Now we have a path from a user to the transaction to the product. Another user on another transaction is another path in this very simplistic graph. Now that we have a graph, we can apply graph deep learning, like graph neural networks, which is a way to generalize deep learning to graph-structured data, and just train over that to get an accurate prediction.

items.question: Why do you favor relational deep learning over manually engineered features for database prediction tasks?
items.object: The advantages and limits of relational deep learning over manual feature engineering
items.answer: Two things happen. The first is you don't have to do manual feature engineering anymore. It's much faster, it requires much less effort to train these models. The second is your models are more accurate. The answer is similar to what happens in computer vision. If you're saying, "I am a human, I know what a car is, so I will build perfect features that detect whether there is a car on the image or not. I know cars, I drive them, I'm such a car expert, I can build the best features for detecting cars," nobody in their right mind claims that. But in machine learning, data science, prediction, people are still saying, "No, I'm the domain expert, I'll engineer the features." Your features are just some arbitrary human-biased summary statistic of your data that you dreamt up, put as a feature in your training table, retrain the model, and then saw whether that increased the accuracy or not. A neural network that trains with gradient descent is able to do so much more nuanced, almost like feature discovery, by attending over this graph to extract much more signal. So we see these double-digit increases in model accuracy because the neural network is able to extract more signal out of the raw data. And I will just, for full transparency, if you are working on a super simple problem that falls on a line, then no neural network is ever going to be better than a linear model. I cannot guarantee that always you will get better performance because sometimes the data is linear. If you happen to train the linear model to it, you already have good performance. There's nothing more you can do. But the majority of the data is not linear, is much more complex, and that's where the benefit happens. That's the key idea behind relational deep learning: now we can have neural networks just learn directly on the raw database data. Don't need to build these manual feature pipelines and feature stores that are super painful and lead to bugs and inconsistencies and information leakage and time travel, and make putting models in production super hard. Rather, just bring the raw data, have a neural network, and get better results that way. That's the philosophy and the reasons why we are doing this.

items.question: How do you think about what a relational deep learning framework can predict from connected database tables?
items.object: The predictive capabilities of relational deep learning
items.answer: The way I describe the framework right now, it's very generic in a sense that you can bring any set of tables, any set of connections between them, any set of columns. The underlying mathematical representation remains the same, and of course the underlying graph changes, but the graph neural network or the graph transformer can be applied to that. What would you want to predict? It depends on the data. If you have a transaction graph, for example, where we see great results is fraud: all kinds of fraud detection, anti-money laundering, account-level fraud, transaction-level fraud. It works beautifully. You just bring this heterogeneous multi-tabular data together and learn over it what fraud is. Fraud is interesting because it's so non-stationary; fraudsters are trying to game the system all the time. So, as a machine learning engineer, you are always behind. Your model is always deteriorating, and you're like, "Okay, how do I design the next feature?" You have a neural network if you just take the signal directly out of the raw data. Fraud is an example you can think of as a classification task. Then you can think a lot around regression-type tasks, for example, customer behavior in terms of customer churn, the next best action, things like that. And then you can also think about, in graph terms, link prediction, so predicting links between two types of entities. The canonical task there is a recommender system, because it's predicting a link between the customer, the user, and the product. We've seen great uses of this in recommender systems for ads, product recommendations, and things like that.

items.question: How do you understand the scope of what the tabular machine learning community works on?
items.object: Tabular machine learning
items.answer: When we say tabular data and tabular machine learning, this is the community that works on single-table problems. The data has already been flattened, pre-formatted, summarized to fit in a single table.
quotes: When we say tabular data and tabular machine learning, this is the community that works on single-table problems. The data has already been flattened, pre-formatted, summarized to fit in a single table.

rubrics.text: The response states that tabular machine learning takes as its starting point data that has already been transformed to fit into a single table.

items.question: Why do you see multi-table machine learning as a more important problem to solve than single-table machine learning?
items.object: Single-table versus multi-table machine learning
items.answer: What we see is that these models and architectures and deep learning didn't really displace XGBoost. XGBoost is still the workhorse. Maybe on individual examples, you can do better, but it's still the workhorse. The reason I'm less interested in this single-table problem is because that's not the right problem to solve. I don't know any organization that has all their data in a single table. The hard part, and where the information gets lost, is when you go from this rich relational structure into the single table. Once you are in a single table, then we are talking almost like second-order effects. Did you use this architecture? Did you use that architecture? Did you use this tabular model or this tabular foundation model or not? All the information is there in that single table and all the methods are about equally good at extracting it. I think where the difference happens is if you actually make a step back and say, "Hey, the single-table model is not the hard part. It's not where you need to go. You need to go to the multi-table setting because that's truly the raw data you have. It's not some summarized, featurized data; it's the raw data. There is much more signal there that got drawn out when the data got flattened into a single table." To me, single-table problems are solved. The differences are second-order effects. What is unsolved is the multi-table problem. That's where the wins are being hidden.

items.question: What gap in machine learning benchmarks were you trying to address with Stanford's RelBench?
items.object: The lack of multi-table benchmarks and the motivation for RelBench
items.answer: Actually, there is quite a lot of single-table data out there because of all the history of machine learning. Even when people develop new benchmarks from raw data, they just release that single table because everyone learns on the single table. So, what we did at Stanford, we were like, "Okay, so where is a multi-table benchmark?" There's no multi-table benchmark. Even if you look at Kaggle, out of thousands of competitions on Kaggle, there are four that are multi-table. All the others are features already engineered for you, there's a single table, and you start bagging and boosting and creating tricks until you win. So, we created a benchmark at Stanford by collecting and curating open multi-tabular data sets that we were able to find on the web. We call it RelBench. We have now two versions of RelBench. It's about 40 different predictive tasks over, I think, about 10 or 15 different databases.
quotes: Actually, there is quite a lot of single-table data out there because of all the history of machine learning. Even when people develop new benchmarks from raw data, they just release that single table because everyone learns on the single table.

So, what we did at Stanford, we were like, "Okay, so where is a multi-table benchmark?" There's no multi-table benchmark. Even if you look at Kaggle, out of thousands of competitions on Kaggle, there are four that are multi-table. All the others are features already engineered for you, there's a single table, and you start bagging and boosting and creating tricks until you win.

So, we created a benchmark at Stanford by collecting and curating open multi-tabular data sets that we were able to find on the web. We call it RelBench. We have now two versions of RelBench. It's about 40 different predictive tasks over, I think, about 10 or 15 different databases.

items.question: How do you make your database model's explanations readable and useful to people?
items.object: Explaining database-model predictions through attention and large language models
items.answer: What we do is, because the model is fully differentiable, we can basically run the model backwards and see what tables, what columns, what cells the model is attending over. We get this structure-based explanation, but then we use a large language model to say, "Here's where the attention is, this is what the columns are and this is what the semantics is," and then we generate a text-based explanation that is super readable and super friendly.

items.question: How do you assess your predictive models’ ability to work across different scales of data?

items.question: How do you think about the computational cost of using AI models to make predictions over enterprise database data?
items.object: The computational cost of AI models for enterprise database predictions
items.answer: At the end, what is being paid for is compute. What we are really doing is taking that workload from the CPU to the GPU. The amount of GPU compute is larger because it's computed over the raw data, not over the summaries generated on the CPU. That's what the cost is in the end. Of course, these models are not in trillions of parameters. They are billion-parameter types. They can be quite small, so they're actually quite efficient and cheap to run because the reason we are making predictions is to make decisions. Our recommender is making decisions about what to show to every user. The speed of those decisions is tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, millions of times per second. So performance and cost really matter.

items.question: Where do you see the biggest bottleneck in getting business value from your predictive modeling technology?

items.question: How do you think about the benefits of post-training and fine-tuning foundation models for structured data?
items.object: Post-training and task-specific fine-tuning of foundation models for structured data
items.answer: That's something we are deeply looking into right now. I would say there's several reasons why to post-train. One reason you would want to post-train even in the in-context learning scenario is to better learn the distribution of the underlying data, to better understand the distribution of the underlying data so that prediction gets better encoded and prediction later will be more accurate. So that's one reason you would want to train in a task-agnostic way over the underlying data to better capture distributions, to better learn priors. Another reason why you would want to fine-tune is for cost reasons. Because if I fine-tune for a specific task, I don't need to do ICL. Now my context is much smaller. I don't need to bring in the label data. I just bring in the entity I want to predict on. The attention is smaller, it's faster, it's cheaper to run. If I have large amounts of data, the model can learn a lot from it. I would say there's a spectrum, there's a continuum of what you can do, and the benefits of it are different depending on where on this continuum you sit.

items.question: Why do you think coding agents need higher-level APIs to perform predictive modeling effectively?
items.object: Higher-level APIs for coding agents performing predictive modeling
items.answer: What we see is that coding agents require a proper abstraction and a proper infrastructure to be effective. For example, you could say, "Hey, why don't I just give this modeling task to Claude Code, and Claude Code will build the model for me. What's the big deal?" When we do that, what we see—we've run this internally—is that these models write thousands of lines of code, but there are super-subtle data science mistakes. For example, we've done this together with Expedia, when it was account-level fraud. A mistake the agent made was that when it created features for that given account, it aggregated the transactions till midnight, not till the current time. It said, "Today is April 30th, so we'll use the data up to midnight of April 30th," not actually saying, "Hey, it's actually 10:00 a.m. on April 30th. We can only use data up to here." That's information leakage. Another mistake it made was that it did it at the transaction level instead of the account level. These are subtle mistakes that really require the human in there. But if you give it a higher-level API, then it's able to do the same work in about 50 lines of code. No mistakes.

items.question: Why do you think agent-friendly APIs matter for agents building machine learning models?
items.object: Agent-friendly APIs for autonomous model building
items.answer: What I'm saying is agents can autonomously maybe make two steps, but not 100 steps. So now when I ask it for a task, I can say, "Hey, here's PyTorch. Go build me the model." That takes 1,000 lines of code to build a model with PyTorch. I could say, "Here's XGBoost. Build me a model." That takes about 500 lines of code, engineering features and so on. Or I can say, "Using the Kumo API, go build me the model." That only takes 50 lines of code. If you think of this analogy of steps, lines of code is maybe like two steps. Five hundred lines of code is 20 steps. You can get quite lost navigating 20 steps in this sense. I think the observation is more general: for agents to be effective, they need APIs that are agent-friendly.
